title: A tale of two domains: how PIF7 controls hypocotyl growth
content: In addition to its influence on photosynthesis, light acts as a power signal for plants. One major input plants detect is the ratio of red (R) to far-red (FR) light. Sunny days have a high R:FR ratio, while shade from cloud cover or nearby vegetation is enriched for FR light, leading to low R:FR perception. Light-sensing PHYTOCHROME (Phy) A and B act to trigger downstream responses to either high or low R:FR (Smith and Whitelam 1997). PhyB is critical for shade avoidance syndrome (SAS), which occurs when high levels of FR (low R:FR) are detected, shifting the light sensor from its active (Pfr) state to the inactive state (Pr) (Leivar et al. 2008). In low R:FR light, SAS-promoting transcription factors (TFs), such as PHYTOCHROME INTERACTING FACTORS (PIFs), bind to PIF-binding E-box (PBE) motifs in the promoters of various shade-responsive genes, activating various processes such as auxin biosynthesis, hypocotyl and petiole elongation, and leaf hyponasty (Roig-Villanova et al. 2007; Lorrain et al. 2008; Hornitschek et al. 2012; Hussain et al. 2022). In high R light (high R:FR), PhyB binds to PIFs, rapidly leading to their phosphorylation and degradation, making PIF activity highly sensitive to changes in light conditions (Park et al. 2004; Al-Sady et al. 2006; Leivar and Quail 2011). This PhyB-PIF interaction occurs at the PIF Active Phytochrome B-binding (APB) region (Shen et al. 2008). In PIF3, the APB is required for hypocotyl elongation but not for early gene expression changes, suggesting that PIF3's full activity may be more complex than acting solely as a TF (Al-Sady et al. 2006).
